title: numberwords language rule spec
description:
Validates a language rule spec as implemented today by reference/engine.py -- see docs/spec-format.md for the prose description. This schema is deliberately DESCRIPTIVE, not aspirational: it encodes the format that currently exists, and nothing that has only been proposed. Extend it in the same PR that extends the format, never ahead of it.

Validation runs against the JSON normalisation of the YAML file (docs/spec-format.md: 'YAML for authoring; it normalises to JSON as the IR'). That matters because YAML gives integer lexicon keys while JSON object keys are always strings -- hence the numeric-string key patterns below.

meta.description: Language identity and the declared supported range.

code.description: ISO 639-3 code, e.g. 'lus' for Mizo. Three lowercase letters -- 639-3 rather than 639-1 so languages without a two-letter code are representable.

version.description: Spec version, independent of any package version.

supports.description: The inclusive range this spec claims to convert. The engine refuses anything outside it rather than guessing.

orthography.description: Optional. The writing system this spec's lexicon is spelled in, e.g. 'missionary' for Mizo. Diacritics depend on it, so a different orthography changes the lexicon throughout.

sources.description: Where the numeral data came from -- dictionary, grammar, or named native speaker. Required, and required non-empty: CONTRIBUTING.md forbids asserting linguistic facts without a source, and an unsourced spec is exactly what that rule exists to prevent.

lexicon.description: The atomic number words, grouped into tables. Table names (units, scales, teens, ...) are open -- languages differ in which groupings they need.

additionalProperties.description: One lexicon table, keyed by the integer value each entry represents.

propertyNames.description: Keys are the numeric value, as a string after JSON normalisation.

additionalProperties.description: One entry, holding every grammatical form of that word. Field names are open by design: docs/spec-format.md asks that each be named after the condition that selects it (Mizo units use standalone/bound; its scales use standalone/multiplied, which is a different condition).

connector.description: Optional. A connector number_to_text writes into every number from `min` up, before its final addend -- the innermost {remainder}. Mizo's 'leh' (#27 Q-M). A property of the whole number rather than of a rule, which is why it is declared here once rather than written into templates. The word must also be listed in parse.connectors, or the canonical spelling would not parse back; the engine checks that at load. Its placement also says where else a connector may idiomatically stand -- before any addend -- which is what the vector generator certifies.

placement.description: Where the connector goes. One placement exists because one has been needed.

min.description: The smallest number that gets the connector.

stacking.description: Optional, input only. A rule keyed by a scale at or above `accepted_from`, whose template writes its multiplier as a word, also accepts a whole numeral in that slot, read by the same rules from scales below its own -- Mizo's `nuai za hnih` is 10^5 x 200 (#27 rule 6). The multiplier binds greedily: of the readings stacking allows, the one whose outermost stacked multiplier takes in the most words wins, and a tie is still an error. number_to_text never writes a stacked form.

accepted_from.description: The smallest scale whose word may head a stacked form. Compared with the rule's scale, not with the value the form stands for (#65).

emit.description: Stacked forms are accepted and never written. Required so the declaration says so itself.

rules.description: number_to_text takes the largest scale any emitting rule is keyed by that is not above the number, then the first rule at that scale, in order, whose `multiplier` and `condition` both hold. Order is significant only between rules of the same scale. text_to_number parses by recursive descent over all of them.

name.description: Identifies the rule in tests, errors and review discussion. Not used for matching.

scale.description: The power of ten this rule consumes (CLDR RBNF's base value). The rule sees multiplier = n // scale and remainder = n % scale.

multiplier.description: Optional. A fixed multiplier: the rule applies only when n // scale is this value. For a rule whose template does not write the multiplier -- Mizo's bare 'sâwm' for 10 -- this is how a parser learns it. A condition cannot do that job: it can check a multiplier, not supply one (#65). The engine refuses, at load, a rule that neither writes its multiplier outside a [...] segment nor fixes it here.

condition.description: Optional extra test over the variables `multiplier` and `remainder`. Evaluated by a restricted AST walker in engine.py -- comparisons, and/or, names and integer constants only. NOT eval(). Anything outside that subset raises rather than executing.

output.description: The rendering this rule produces: literal text, {table[key].field} lexicon placeholders whose key is multiplier, remainder or a literal integer, and {remainder} -- the remainder rendered by the same rules. A [...] segment is dropped when the remainder is zero; {remainder} may only appear inside one, and segments do not nest (the engine enforces those two). The pattern enforces that every brace group is a well-formed placeholder and every bracket closes, so a typo like {units[multiplier]} fails validation instead of failing at render time.

emit.description: Optional. 'never' makes the rule accepted when parsing but never produced by number_to_text -- e.g. Mizo's compound-tens shorthand 'hnih thum' for 23.

scope.description: Optional, and only on an 'emit: never' rule. 'whole' accepts the rule for an entire input only, never as the remainder inside a longer number: without it Mizo's shorthand would let 'za hnih khat' parse as 121 (#65).

parse.description: Hints for the reverse direction. Every flag here loosens matching only; none of it changes what number_to_text emits. Optional -- engine.py treats a missing parse section as all-defaults.

case_insensitive.description: Lowercase input and lexicon before comparing.

strip_diacritics.description: Remove combining marks from input and lexicon before comparing, so ASCII-typed input matches. Applied to both sides -- applying it to input alone would stop it matching the lexicon.

word_separators.description: Non-whitespace strings the input may also be split on, e.g. ['-']. Unicode White_Space is a separator in every language and is applied by the engine rather than declared here (#46), so listing ' ' would be redundant -- and would let a target split on only the declared list, ignore the whitespace rule, and still pass every vector. Omit the property entirely for a language whose only separators are whitespace.

accepted_forms.description: Extra lexicon fields a freestanding single-word phrase may match, keyed by lexicon table. The field a template names always matches, so list only the extras: Mizo's 'units': ['bound'] also accepts the bound form of a lone digit, whose template names 'standalone'. Omit the section entirely for exact matching -- a language whose entries have one form each declares nothing. Leniency applies only where the whole input is a single word; that rule belongs to the engine, being about ambiguity rather than about any one language.

connectors.description: Filler words dropped when parsing, wherever they fall, e.g. Mizo 'leh'. A tolerance, not a claim about meaning. Where a connector is written on output is grammar.connector's business.

aliases.description: Irregular spelling variants that normalisation flags cannot express, mapped variant -> canonical. Prefer a parse flag where one applies: a flag is one line and covers every word, an alias list grows per word.

examples.description: Optional hand-written {number, text} pairs. These are independent ground truth -- written by hand, not generated from the engine -- so they catch a spec change that silently alters output.
